examinerBank.question: Walk me through your differential for this patient's confusion and hyperglycaemia, and how the biochemistry helps you distinguish between them.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Top of the list is HHS given glucose 42.8 mmol/L, calculated osmolality 356 mOsm/kg, only mild ketosis (0.4 mmol/L) and near-normal pH/bicarbonate — the picture is dominated by profound dehydration and hyperosmolality rather than ketoacidosis. DKA is next but argued against by the minimal ketosis and only mildly low bicarbonate, and absence of Kussmaul breathing. Sepsis-associated delirium alone doesn't explain the glucose/osmolality derangement, though the pneumonia is clearly the precipitant. Stroke is unlikely given no focal neurological signs, and the metabolic picture is sufficient to explain the presentation.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks for ranked differential with reasoning tied to specific glucose/ketone/pH/osmolality values, not just naming HHS.

examinerBank.question: Why does this patient have such profound hyperglycaemia and dehydration but only mild ketosis, unlike a typical DKA presentation?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: He has type 2 diabetes with residual endogenous insulin secretion — enough circulating insulin to suppress hepatic ketogenesis and lipolysis, but not enough to control hepatic glucose output and peripheral glucose uptake. This allows glucose to climb to extreme levels while ketone production stays low, so the clinical picture is dominated by osmotic diuresis and dehydration rather than acidosis.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the mechanistic distinction (residual insulin sufficient to block lipolysis/ketogenesis but not hyperglycaemia) — the core pathophysiology pearl distinguishing HHS from DKA.

examinerBank.question: Why is initial fluid management in HHS approached more cautiously than in DKA, and what could go wrong if you correct too quickly?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: HHS patients, often elderly, have extreme serum osmolality; too-rapid correction of osmolality or glucose can cause a large osmotic shift of water into brain cells, precipitating cerebral oedema. Fluid deficits (often 8-10L) should be replaced over 24-48 hours with gradual glucose decline of about 4-6 mmol/L/hour, and insulin is often delayed or given at a lower rate than in DKA until fluids alone stop dropping the glucose.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Should mention cerebral oedema risk from rapid osmotic correction and the slower, fluids-first approach distinct from DKA protocol.

examinerBank.question: His serum sodium comes back at 152 mmol/L in the context of glucose 42.8 mmol/L. How do you interpret this, and does it change your fluid choice?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Sodium must be corrected for the hyperglycaemia (add roughly 2-4 mmol/L to measured sodium for every 5.5 mmol/L glucose above normal) — his true corrected sodium is even higher, confirming severe hypertonic dehydration. This supports starting with 0.9% saline for volume resuscitation; if corrected sodium remains very high once volume is restored, a switch to a more hypotonic fluid may be considered, but initial resuscitation should still prioritise restoring circulating volume.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Tests understanding of corrected sodium calculation and fluid choice reasoning in hyperosmolar states — partial credit for correctly identifying severe hypertonicity even without exact formula recall.

framework: decompensated hyperglycaemia presentation: characterise tempo and osmotic symptoms → confirm severity/precipitant → exclude DKA mimic → classify diabetes type → screen for precipitant and complications → individualise management and follow-up

patient.name: Muzi Ngcobo
patient.personality: drowsy and slow to answer, family (daughter) fills in most of the history, mildly confused but rousable
patient.openingLine: (patient is drowsy; daughter speaks) Doctor, my father has been so tired and confused these last few days, he's hardly drinking anything even though he says he's thirsty.

presentingComplaint: 3-day history of progressive confusion, lethargy and reduced oral intake in a known type 2 diabetic, brought in by family after he became difficult to rouse this morning

history.fact: Symptoms have been building gradually over about 1-2 weeks, with rapid worsening of confusion in the last 2-3 days
Was getting up 4-5 times a night to pass urine and drinking large amounts of water before he became too drowsy to drink
Over the past 2 days has barely been eating or drinking because he 'didn't feel like it' and family thought he had flu
Increasingly muddled over the last 2 days, not recognising his grandchildren this morning, daughter says 'he's not himself'
No deliberate weight change noted recently by family, though he looks more sunken-eyed than usual
No vomiting, no abdominal pain, no nausea reported
No rapid or laboured breathing noticed by the family, no unusual breath smell
Had a productive cough and fevers for about a week before this, thought to be a 'chest cold'; no urinary burning reported by family
Known type 2 diabetic for 12 years, previously on metformin and gliclazide, control has been 'up and down' — last clinic HbA1c around 9.5%
Ran out of his diabetes tablets about 3 weeks ago and did not manage to get to the clinic for a refill
Also takes hydrochlorothiazide for blood pressure; no steroids, no antipsychotics
Known hypertensive for 15 years; no known kidney disease, no previous stroke or heart attack
HIV status unknown, has never been tested; not sexually active for many years per daughter
No known TB contact, no prior TB treatment; the cough and fever this past week raise concern
Lives with his daughter and grandchildren in KwaMashu; retired, non-smoker, drinks alcohol rarely
Two siblings also have type 2 diabetes; no family history of type 1 diabetes or early-onset diabetes
No previous admissions for diabetic emergencies, no known prior DKA or hypoglycaemic episodes

examination.general: Elderly man, drowsy but rousable to voice (GCS 12/15, E3V4M5), profound dehydration with dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor. No Kussmaul breathing, no ketotic (fruity) breath odour. Looks chronically unwell.
examination.respiratory: Trachea central, no increased work of breathing, no Kussmaul pattern. Right basal crackles with reduced air entry, dull to percussion at right base — suggestive of consolidation.
examination.cardio: Tachycardic, normal heart sounds, no murmurs, JVP not visible (likely low due to dehydration), peripheries cool with delayed capillary refill (~3s), weak thready pulses.
examination.abdo: Soft, non-tender, no guarding, no organomegaly, bowel sounds present, no rigidity.
examination.neuro: GCS 12/15 (confused, opens eyes to voice, localises to pain), no focal neurological deficit, no meningism, plantars downgoing, no papilloedema. No signs of raised intracranial pressure.

investigations.name: Blood ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate)
investigations.result: 0.4 mmol/L (mildly elevated, not in ketoacidosis range)

investigations.name: Venous blood gas / bicarbonate
investigations.result: pH 7.34, HCO3- 20 mmol/L (mild acidosis from dehydration/sepsis, not primary ketoacidosis)

investigations.name: U&E/creatinine
investigations.result: Na+ 152 mmol/L (corrected for glucose), K+ 5.1 mmol/L, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 210 µmol/L (acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal)

investigations.name: Urine dipstick/ketones
investigations.result: Glucose 4+, trace ketones, no nitrites, no leucocytes

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Right lower zone consolidation consistent with pneumonia — likely precipitant

investigations.name: Blood and urine cultures
investigations.result: Sent, pending at time of assessment

investigations.name: ECG
investigations.result: Sinus tachycardia, no acute ischaemic changes, no peaked T waves despite K+ 5.1

for: known poorly controlled type 2 diabetic who stopped medication

against: ketones only mildly elevated (0.4 mmol/L, DKA typically >3 mmol/L)
bicarbonate only mildly low (20 vs typical DKA <15)
clinical picture dominated by profound dehydration/hyperosmolality rather than acidosis

differentials.dx: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy / delirium from pneumonia alone
against: does not explain glucose of 42.8 mmol/L or osmolality of 356
hyperosmolar state itself is sufficient to cause the confusion
glucose and osmolality abnormalities far exceed what simple sepsis delirium would produce

for: altered consciousness in an elderly hypertensive patient
against: biochemical picture fully explains the clinical state
symptoms improved framework points to metabolic cause first

pathophys.polyuria and polydipsia (preceding the c: Sustained hyperglycaemia exceeds the renal tubular reabsorptive threshold for glucose (~10-11 mmol/L), causing glycosuria and osmotic diuresis with obligate water loss, triggering compensatory thirst
pathophys.altered mental status / confusion: Extreme hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg) causes cellular dehydration of neurons and shrinkage of brain volume, disrupting neuronal function; severity of encephalopathy correlates directly with degree of osmolality elevation
pathophys.profound dehydration with minimal ketosi: Residual endogenous insulin secretion in type 2 diabetes is sufficient to suppress hepatic ketogenesis and lipolysis even as hepatic glucose output and impaired peripheral uptake drive severe hyperglycaemia, so the osmotic diuretic effect dominates over ketoacidosis
pathophys.acute kidney injury: Profound volume depletion from osmotic diuresis leads to pre-renal hypoperfusion of the kidneys, reducing glomerular filtration and raising urea/creatinine, which in turn worsens glucose and osmolality clearance in a vicious cycle
pathophys.precipitating infection (pneumonia): Acute infective stress triggers a surge of counter-regulatory hormones (cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon) that increase hepatic gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, tipping a poorly controlled type 2 diabetic into decompensation, compounded here by medication non-adherence

staging: HHS with severe hyperosmolality (356 mOsm/kg); AKI (likely pre-renal, KDIGO stage 2 based on creatinine rise); background poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 11.2%)

immediate: Admit to a monitored/high-care bed, insert two large-bore IV lines
Cautious IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride — correct estimated deficit (often 8-10L) slowly over 24-48 hours to avoid rapid osmotic shifts and cerebral oedema
Hourly neurological observations and GCS monitoring given altered mental status

Start low-dose IV insulin infusion only once fluid resuscitation underway and glucose stops falling with fluids alone, or immediately if ketones significant — typical fixed-rate ~0.05 units/kg/hr (lower than DKA protocol)
Aim for gradual glucose fall (~4-6 mmol/L/hr) and gradual osmolality correction to avoid cerebral oedema/osmotic demyelination
Hourly/2-hourly capillary glucose, and monitor electrolytes (especially potassium) closely with replacement as needed
Identify and treat precipitant — empirical antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia per local protocol, blood/urine/sputum cultures sent
VTE prophylaxis (HHS carries high thrombosis risk) unless contraindicated
definitive: Restart/optimise diabetes therapy once stabilised — reintroduce metformin once renal function and hydration recover, reassess need for insulin vs oral agents
Address medication non-adherence — link to chronic medication supply, consider community health worker/clinic support given missed refill was the key precipitant
Diabetes education for patient and family regarding sick-day rules and warning signs of decompensation
Treat pneumonia fully per SA STG with appropriate antibiotic course and monitor for resolution
supportive: Nutrition support and dietitian referral once oral intake safe
Involve family/daughter in adherence planning and glucose monitoring at home
Screen for underlying complications once stable: fundoscopy, foot assessment, urine ACR, lipogram
Physiotherapy/mobility support given prolonged bed rest risk in an elderly patient
followUp: Diabetes clinic follow-up within 1-2 weeks post-discharge to reassess regimen and adherence
Repeat renal function to confirm resolution of AKI
Annual retinal screening and foot risk stratification if not recently done
Reinforce sick-day management rules — never stop medication outright, seek care early with reduced intake or illness
TB symptom screen given cough at presentation — arrange sputum GeneXpert if cough persists after pneumonia treatment

stationChecklist.item: Characterises the presentation: tempo (days-weeks), osmotic symptoms preceding admission, and how the patient came to present via decompensation/confusion rather than routine follow-up
stationChecklist.answer: Gradual polyuria/polydipsia over 1-2 weeks culminating in confusion and reduced intake over the last 2-3 days
stationChecklist.why: Distinguishes an acute crisis from an incidental glucose finding and frames the case within the symptom-to-crisis framework

stationChecklist.item: Screens for ketosis symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing) to help distinguish HHS from DKA at the bedside
stationChecklist.answer: No vomiting, no abdominal pain, no rapid/laboured breathing reported
stationChecklist.why: Absence of ketotic symptoms alongside the biochemistry supports HHS over DKA as the working diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Actively hunts for a precipitant — infection, medication non-adherence, new illness
stationChecklist.answer: Cough and fever for a week (pneumonia) plus 3 weeks off his diabetes tablets
stationChecklist.why: HHS is almost always precipitated by infection, non-adherence, or new illness; identifying and treating the precipitant is essential to recovery

stationChecklist.item: Establishes diabetes history: known duration, type, prior control, current medications
stationChecklist.answer: 12-year type 2 diabetic on metformin and gliclazide, HbA1c ~9.5% previously, ran out of tablets 3 weeks ago
stationChecklist.why: Confirms background type 2 diabetes and clarifies why decompensation occurred (non-adherence)

stationChecklist.item: Screens for comorbidities and secondary contributors: hypertension, other medications (thiazides), HIV status, TB symptoms
stationChecklist.answer: Hypertensive on hydrochlorothiazide (can worsen glycaemic control/dehydration); HIV never tested; cough raises TB concern
stationChecklist.why: KZN practice mandates HIV/TB cross-screening in any diabetic presentation, and identifies drugs contributing to dehydration/hyperglycaemia

stationChecklist.item: Assesses hydration status and haemodynamic stability (mucous membranes, skin turgor, capillary refill, postural/supine vitals)
stationChecklist.answer: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardic, hypotensive, delayed capillary refill — profound dehydration
stationChecklist.why: Degree of dehydration guides fluid resuscitation volume and rate, the cornerstone of initial HHS management

stationChecklist.item: Performs a focused neurological assessment including GCS and screens for focal deficit to exclude an alternative cause of altered mental status
stationChecklist.answer: GCS 12/15, no focal neurological deficit, no meningism
stationChecklist.why: Confirms hyperosmolality as the likely cause of confusion and excludes stroke/meningitis as competing differentials

stationChecklist.item: Examines for a source of infection/precipitant (chest, abdomen, urine, skin/feet)
stationChecklist.answer: Right basal crackles and dullness consistent with pneumonia; no abdominal tenderness; feet without active ulceration
stationChecklist.why: Localises the infective precipitant driving decompensation and screens for diabetic foot sepsis as an alternative source

stationChecklist.item: Generates a ranked differential distinguishing HHS from DKA, sepsis-alone delirium, and stroke, with reasoning linked to glucose, ketones, pH, and osmolality
stationChecklist.why: Core diagnostic reasoning step of the framework — HHS is a diagnosis of exclusion/pattern-recognition against its closest mimics

stationChecklist.item: Requests the confirmatory panel: glucose, calculated serum osmolality, blood ketones, venous blood gas/bicarbonate, U&E
stationChecklist.answer: Glucose 42.8 mmol/L, osmolality 356 mOsm/kg, ketones 0.4 mmol/L, pH 7.34/HCO3 20, Na+ 152, K+ 5.1, urea 22, creatinine 210
stationChecklist.why: This panel is what defines HHS (severe hyperglycaemia + hyperosmolality + minimal ketosis/acidosis) versus DKA

stationChecklist.item: Investigates for the precipitant: chest X-ray, FBC/CRP, cultures, HIV test
stationChecklist.answer: CXR shows right lower zone consolidation; WCC and CRP raised; HIV negative; cultures pending
stationChecklist.why: Identifying and treating the underlying precipitant is essential — HHS will not resolve or will recur if the trigger is missed

stationChecklist.item: Outlines cautious fluid resuscitation as first priority, with slow, staged correction to avoid cerebral oedema, before or alongside low-dose insulin
stationChecklist.answer: IV 0.9% saline to correct large fluid deficit gradually over 24-48h; low-dose insulin infusion once glucose plateaus or ketones significant
stationChecklist.why: HHS management differs critically from DKA — fluids come first and correction must be slower given the risk of rapid osmotic shifts in elderly patients

stationChecklist.item: Describes monitoring plan: hourly glucose/neuro observations, electrolyte (especially potassium) monitoring, VTE prophylaxis
stationChecklist.answer: Hourly GCS and glucose, 2-hourly electrolytes, potassium replacement as needed, VTE prophylaxis given high thrombosis risk in HHS
stationChecklist.why: HHS carries high morbidity/mortality from cerebral oedema, arrhythmia from potassium shifts, and thrombosis if unmonitored

stationChecklist.item: Plans definitive/follow-up care: treat pneumonia fully, address medication non-adherence, arrange diabetes clinic follow-up and complication screening
stationChecklist.answer: Complete antibiotic course, restart oral agents once renal function recovers, link to chronic medication supply, diabetes clinic review in 1-2 weeks
stationChecklist.why: Prevents recurrence by addressing both the precipitant and the root cause (non-adherence) with structured follow-up
